answer.answer:
Robotic building rests on four things at once, and the evidence treats them as requirements rather than options: a machine capable of the motion, notably a robot arm; a path plan derived from geometry and from the robot knowing where it is; a product designed for it, meaning extensive prefabrication and standardised, unified components; and a structured, controlled environment, which on site usually means enclosing the work under a mobile factory. Beyond the hardware and the information chain, robotic assembly is also reported to depend on the delivery model, business model and work culture of the firm doing it, and human-robot collaborative work depends on skilled staff and on compliance with robot safety standards. What it brings back is faster schedules, fewer errors and, for geometrically complex work, a real cost advantage. Watch the organisational and regulatory side: the controlled-enclosure condition appears in only one coded case, so most robotic building in the record is happening without it, and the approval route for on-site printing runs through an alternative-means pathway rather than a settled code.

**The machine and the motion.** Robotic assembly (PR4) is the hinge enabler here, and its dependency neighbourhood is fully enumerated: four inbound and six outbound edges. On the hardware side the relation is stated in both directions, a robot arm enables robotic assembly [1] (DEP11) and robotic assembly requires a robot arm [2] (DEP24), both peer-reviewed [1]. Robotic assembly (PR4) is activated in 13 of the 50 coded cases and the robot arm (RE2) in 23.

**The information chain.** Path planning (PR12) is a directional precondition, not a correlate: path planning enables robotic assembly, and is described as a precondition for it, on peer-reviewed evidence [3] [2]. Path planning itself carries three inbound and three outbound edges: it is driven by algorithmic geometry (RE1, DEP7) and by AI and deep reinforcement learning for autonomous path planning [2] (RE8, DEP3), it requires 3D point-cloud geometry [2] (CO16, DEP30), and it has localisation via onboard sensors as a fundamental prerequisite for autonomous operation [2] (RE4, DEP39). One edge is a constraint rather than an enabler: reliable GNSS signals are typically unavailable indoors, which constrains the choice of localisation method [2] (RI5, DEP44). Upstream of all this sits the design-to-machine chain, reached through fabrication information modelling (CO3), which links BIM-based design to digital fabrication via a digital chain [2], through manufacturing information generated independently of the machine system [2] (RE13), and through integrated information management for integrated automated construction [2] (RE9), all into AR9, which is activated in 44 of 50 cases and in turn reduces dependence on site labour [2] (VA1).

**The product.** Robotic assembly has an explicit product-side precondition: automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials [2] (PR2, DEP55), and Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components [2] (AT7, DEP88), the first peer-reviewed [3], the second from a book-length source. Standardisation is reinforced by a standard: the base module standard reduces component variety and coordinates design, manufacture and assembly [2] (AT7 to VA7, DEP67). The activation count for prefabrication (PR2) is not in front of me, so I cannot say how many coded cases use it.

**The environment.** For on-site work the enclosure comes first: on-site DFAB (PR8) has the mobile factory (CO12) as a precondition, because environments need to be much more structured and controlled before construction robots can take over [4] (DEP41). The enclosure pays twice: all-weather cover allows welding and assembly to proceed in a normal manner even in rain [2] (DEP42) and a climbing all-weather roof with overhead delivery greatly increases productivity and stabilises process and quality [2] (DEP56). The alternative to enclosure is a robot that handles the mess itself: a mobile robot with autonomous repositioning and localisation performs on-site digital fabrication [2] (AT9, DEP86). Note the asymmetry in take-up: the mobile factory (CO12) is activated in 1 of 50 coded cases and on-site DFAB (PR8) in 9.

**Organisation, skills and rules.** Robotic assembly depends on the delivery model, business model and work culture, because robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context [5] (RI12, DEP61); RI12 is activated in 16 of 50 cases and carries two inbound edges and none outbound, the other being the finding that adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models [2] (AT8, DEP81).
